To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
BR(μ→e, γ) depends very little on θ13, is typically larger than the present experimental bound, and decreases when leptogenesis is considered.

(a) the seesaw parameter space is scanned in a complete way, including perturbativity; (b) in supersymmetric models, BR(μeγ) depends very weakly on θ13; (c) BR(μe,γ) is typically above the experimental bound, and the bound can be evaded only if the R-matrix is close to diagonal; (d) leptogenesis does no introduce any further dependence of BR(μe γ) on θ13;
the value of θ 13 does not have a significant effect on BR(μ →e, γ), and that this branching ratio is typically above the present experimental upper limit.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the correct and complete treatment of the seesaw model, which is of great importance for the interpretation of the experimental results.
a very simple, but very important, point: the seesaw parameter space must be scanned completely, in order to obtain realistic predictions on the LFV processes.
the consequences of the complete scanning of the seesaw parameter space, including a very simple and straightforward rule to incorporate the requirement of perturbativity, for predictions on LFVs.

the seesaw mechanism does not allow to predict BR(μ →e, γ) in the framework of the MSSM.
the seesaw mechanism, with or without supersymmetry, is not excluded by the current bound on BR(μ →e, γ), even when θ13 is large.
the current experimental upper limit on BR(μ →e,γ) does not allow to constrain θ13, but only the absolute value of the seesaw scale.

, in supersymmetric seesaws, θ13 does not play a relevant role in the prediction of BR(μ→e,γ).
the seesaw mechanism does not predict BR(μ → γ) to be small in the supersymmetric framework.
the seesaw model can be scanned in a very straightforward and complete way, and the dependence of LFV rates on θ13 is very weak, and not at all the way it was thought.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the seesaw is a very predictive theory, which can be scanned in a complete way and in a very simple manner, and the results of such scans should be taken into account when making phenomenological statements.
the seesaw parameter space is much more constrained than it is usually thought, which in turn implies that the predictions for LFV observables should be much sharper than what is usually believed.
a complete scan is necessary for a correct understanding of the parameter space of the seesaw, and the consequences for LFV observables.
